claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer is characterized by a stepwise buildup of genetic alterations in specific oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.
claims.source: This is exemplarily illustrated by the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer where a stepwise buildup of genetic alterations in specific oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes underlies tumor initiation and progression (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: Epigenetic changes, rather than genetic mutations, underlie phenotypic plasticity in cancer.
claims.source: However, with regard to the capacity to disseminate through the tumor microenvironment and establish metastases in distant organ sites, epigenetic changes, rather than genetic mutations, underlie what is the most clinically relevant hallmark of cancer, namely phenotypic plasticity (Varga and Greten, 2017; Teeuwssen and Fodde, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: EMT bestows cancer cells with stem-like plastic characteristics needed to acquire quasi-mesenchymal features at the invasive front.
claims.source: EMT bestows cancer cells with stem-like plastic characteristics (Mani et al., 2008) needed to acquire quasi-mesenchymal features at the invasive front of the primary tumor, disseminate and attain therapy resistance, and to revert back to more epithelial states (mesenchymal to epithelial transition [MET]) at the organ site of metastasis (Brabletz et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Epigenetic activation and silencing of EMT-inducing transcription factors underlies the transient nature of cellular modifications during EMT.
claims.source: Epigenetic activation and silencing of EMT-inducing transcription factors (EMT-TFs) underlies the transient nature of these cellular modifications (Skrypek et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: The 'migrating cancer stem cell' (mCSC) model was first proposed for colon cancer by T. Brabletz.
claims.source: The 'migrating cancer stem cell' (mCSC) model has been first proposed for colon cancer by T. Brabletz (Brabletz et al., 2005), also as a solution to the so-called 'β-catenin paradox' (Fodde and Brabletz, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: In the majority of sporadic colorectal cancer cases, loss of the APC tumor suppressor is predicted to lead to nuclear β-catenin translocation and full-blown Wnt signaling activation.
claims.source: In the majority of sporadic colorectal cancer cases, the rate-limiting loss of the APC tumor suppressor is predicted to lead to nuclear β-catenin translocation and full-blown Wnt signaling activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Tumor cells with nuclear β-catenin represent only a small minority of the primary lesion and tend to cluster at the invasive front of colon carcinomas.
claims.source: Notwithstanding these predictions, tumor cells with nuclear β-catenin represent only a small minority of the primary lesion and tend to cluster non-randomly at the invasive front of colon carcinomas where they gain mesenchymal features to detach and disseminate into the adjacent stromal tissues.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents an observation.

claims.claim: Cues secreted from the tumor microenvironment elicit EMT downstream of full-blown Wnt signaling activation in cells at the invasive front of colon carcinomas.
claims.source: In view of these observations, it is plausible that cues secreted from the tumor microenvironment elicit EMT downstream of full-blown Wnt signaling activation, earmarked by nuclear β-catenin, in a subset of cells located at the invasive front (Brabletz et al., 2005; Fodde and Brabletz, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a plausible hypothesis supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Human immortalized breast cancer cell lines encompass different subpopulations of cells with distinct phenotypic states maintained in a dynamic equilibrium through stochastic transitions.
claims.source: Previously, it was shown that human immortalized breast cancer cell lines encompass different subpopulations of cells with distinct phenotypic states and functional characteristics maintained in a dynamic equilibrium through stochastic transitions between states (Gupta et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: In oral squamous carcinoma cell lines, non-EMT CSCs are proliferative and retain epithelial characteristics, while EMT-competent CSCs are quasi-mesenchymal with increased cellular motility.
claims.source: Similar observations were made in oral squamous carcinoma cell lines where distinct CSC phenotypes are present: whereas non-EMT CSCs are proliferative and retain epithelial characteristics, the EMT-competent CSC fraction is (quasi)mesenchymal and of increased cellular motility (Biddle et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: The mesenchymal CMS4 subtype accounts for approximately 25% of colon cancer cases and is associated with the greatest propensity to form metastases.
claims.source: The mesenchymal CMS4 subtype accounts for approximately 25% of the cases and is associated with the greatest propensity to form metastases.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents established knowledge from CMS classification.

claims.claim: Bona fide tumor cells from stroma-rich cancers have a markedly mesenchymal gene expression pattern.
claims.source: While the CMS4 signature was initially attributed to the presence of tumor-associated stroma and not to a cancer cell-intrinsic property (Calon et al., 2015; Isella et al., 2015), it has been shown that bona fide tumor cells from stroma-rich cancers have a markedly mesenchymal gene expression pattern (Vellinga et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Hybrid E/M or partial EMT cells are thought to be endowed with increased invasive and metastatic capacity.
claims.source: Recent studies on the role of EMT in eliciting phenotypic plasticity in cancer cells have highlighted the relevance of intermediate cellular stages co-expressing both epithelial and mesenchymal genes for tumor progression and metastasis (Jolly et al., 2015; Aiello et al., 2018; Pastushenko et al., 2018). These hybrid E/M or partial EMT cells are thought to be endowed with increased invasive and metastatic capacity.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: SPARC is a matricellular protein involved in the modulation of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions and is known as a prognostic marker in colon cancer.
claims.source: Partial EMT cells, predicted by RNAvelocity to transit between states, are characterized not only by the co-expression of E- and M-specific genes at intermediate levels, but also by increased expression of specific genes like SPARC (Secreted Protein Acidic and Rich in Cysteine, also known as osteonectin), encoding for a matricellular protein involved in the modulation of cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions and known as a prognostic marker in colon cancer (Kim et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claims.claim: SPARC triggers EMT through direct cell-to-cell contact and upregulation of other EMT-inducers like fibronectin (FN1).
claims.source: Importantly, SPARC triggers EMT through direct cell-to-cell contact and upregulation of other EMT-inducers like fibronectin (FN1) (Takigawa et al., 2017), reminiscent of the interactions occurring between parenchymal and stromal cells at the invasive front in colon cancer (Fodde and Brabletz, 2007) where pEMT is expected to underlie plasticity and invasion through the ECM.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claims.claim: CTCs with less pronounced epithelial characteristics are likely to underlie metastasis at distant organ sites.
claims.source: Although current detection methodologies mainly rely on their epithelial features, more recent studies have indicated that CTCs with less pronounced epithelial characteristics are likely to underlie metastasis at distant organ sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents recent findings.

claims.claim: In breast and oral cancer, hybrid E/M tumor cells feature the highest degree of phenotypic plasticity coupling the capacity of undergoing EMT/MET with therapy resistance and other stem cell features.
claims.source: In breast and oral cancer, hybrid E/M tumor cells feature the highest degree of phenotypic plasticity coupling the capacity of undergoing EMT/MET with therapy resistance and other stem cells features (Yu et al., 2013; Biddle et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

results.result: HCT116 and SW480 colon cancer cell lines contain distinct CD44highEpCAMlow (EpCAMlo) subpopulations representing 5.0% ± 2.5% and 16.7% ± 13% of cells, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are directly supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1A with quantified percentages and standard deviations. The gating strategy and methodology are clearly described in supplementary figures.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells exhibit spindle-shaped mesenchymal-like morphology while EpCAMhi cells display compact epithelial morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C4 are supported by phase-contrast microscopy images in Figure 1B showing clear morphological differences between the two subpopulations. The visual evidence is consistent with the described phenotypes.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells from both HCT116 and SW480 produce significantly more liver metastases than EpCAMhi and bulk cells after intrasplenic injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 are supported by quantification data in Figure 1C showing statistically significant differences (p<0.05 and p<0.01) and visual evidence in Figure 1D. Sample sizes are adequate (n=4-9 per group).

results.result: EpCAMlo-derived liver metastases undergo mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET), containing predominantly EpCAMhi cells (>99%).
results.evaluation: Claim C7 is supported by FACS analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B demonstrating the striking plasticity of EpCAMlo cells and their capacity to revert to epithelial phenotype in metastatic lesions.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells have significantly increased migratory and invasive capacity compared to EpCAMhi cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C9 are supported by transwell migration and invasion assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A with statistical significance (p<0.05) from two independent experiments.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells exhibit an EMT gene expression signature with reduced EPCAM and CDH1 expression and increased VIM and ZEB1 expression compared to EpCAMhi cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and immunofluorescence in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, showing consistent EMT marker expression patterns across both cell lines with statistical significance (p<0.05).

results.result: ZEB1 knockdown by shRNA dramatically decreases the percentage of EpCAMlo cells in both HCT116 and SW480 cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by FACS analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C showing substantial reduction in EpCAMlo population after ZEB1 knockdown, establishing ZEB1 as a key driver of the EpCAMlo phenotype.

results.result: All five members of the miR-200 family show significantly reduced expression in EpCAMlo cells compared to EpCAMhi cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D showing statistically significant downregulation (p<0.05 to p<0.001) of all miR-200 family members, consistent with increased ZEB1 expression.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells show decreased mitotic activity compared to EpCAMhi cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C16 is supported by proliferation assay and cell cycle analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F showing reduced proliferation and altered cell cycle distribution in EpCAMlo cells from both lines.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells exhibit chemoresistance to oxaliplatin and 5-FU, showing increased viability and capacity to re-enter the cell cycle after drug treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by MTT viability assays and regrowth assays in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, demonstrating enhanced survival and recovery capacity of EpCAMlo cells across multiple drug concentrations.

results.result: Liver metastases from EpCAMlo cells recapitulate the heterogeneous β-catenin localization pattern observed in primary colon carcinomas.
results.evaluation: Claim C20 is supported by IHC data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and cited references, showing membranous/cytoplasmic β-catenin in the center and nuclear accumulation at the periphery of metastatic lesions.

results.result: Doxycycline-inducible Zeb1 expression in AKP organoids increases EpCAMlo cells in primary tumors but results in only marginal increase in metastases with continuous induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 are supported by FACS analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D and metastasis quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E. The marginal metastasis increase is consistent with the hypothesis that continuous Zeb1 expression inhibits MET required for metastasis formation.

results.result: EpCAMlo cells show high plasticity by reverting to the epithelial EpCAMhi phenotype when cultured, while EpCAMhi cells rarely switch to the mesenchymal state.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C24 are supported by FACS analysis over time in Figure 2A, demonstrating asymmetric bidirectional plasticity with preferential EpCAMlo to EpCAMhi transition.

results.result: Late EpCAMlo cells (cultured >60-100 days) show increased epithelial marker expression, decreased mesenchymal marker expression, and reduced migratory capacity compared to early EpCAMlo cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and migration assay in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, demonstrating time-dependent reversion of EpCAMlo cells toward epithelial phenotype.

results.result: Single-cell clonogenicity assays reveal that the majority of EpCAMlo cells can generate EpCAMhi progeny, while a minority lose plasticity, and most EpCAMhi cells retain epithelial features.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by single-cell clonogenicity data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1, demonstrating heterogeneity in plasticity within the EpCAMlo population and stability of the EpCAMhi phenotype.

results.result: Markov model analysis reveals that EpCAMlo cells have slightly longer doubling times and 4-8 fold higher transition probability to EpCAMhi compared to the reverse transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by Markov model fitting to FACS data shown in Figure 2C. The model provides quantitative estimates of doubling times and transition probabilities, though these are inferred parameters rather than direct measurements.

results.result: Simulation modeling predicts that subclones with lower plasticity gain dominance within a few months in culture.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is supported by simulation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. This is a computational prediction that explains the observed decrease in EpCAMlo percentage over extended culture periods.

results.result: RNAseq analysis identified 152 and 353 differentially regulated genes in HCT116 and SW480 respectively, with only 34 genes common between the two cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by RNAseq differential expression analysis with appropriate statistical thresholds (p.adjusted<0.01, log2FC<-1.5 or >1.5). The limited overlap suggests context-dependent EMT mechanisms.

results.result: Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of combined EpCAMlo expression profiles shows significant associations with EMT regulation, Wnt/β-catenin signaling, human ESC pluripotency, IL8 signaling, and colorectal cancer metastasis.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by IPA results shown in Figure 3B. Despite limited gene overlap between cell lines, common functional pathways emerge, validating the biological relevance of the EpCAMlo phenotype.

results.result: GSK3β inhibitor (Chiron) treatment activates Wnt signaling and increases ZEB1 expression in both cell lines, but only increases EpCAMlo population in HCT116.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by TOP-Flash reporter assay (Figure 3C), FACS analysis (Figure 3D), and immunofluorescence (Figure 3E). The differential response between cell lines suggests additional context-dependent factors regulate EpCAMlo population size.

results.result: Isogenic HCT116 cell lines with increasing β-catenin mutation load show progressive increase in EpCAMlo subpopulation from 3.9% (WT) to 7.9% (heterozygous) to 28.7% (homozygous mutant).
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by FACS analysis in Figure 3F, demonstrating a dose-dependent relationship between β-catenin mutation status and EpCAMlo population size, supporting the role of Wnt signaling in establishing this phenotype.

results.result: Co-localization of nuclear β-catenin and ZEB1 expression was found in 5 out of 25 colon carcinoma cases at the invasive front.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by IHC analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The 20% frequency (5/25) suggests this phenotype occurs in a subset of tumors, validating the clinical relevance of the cell line findings.

results.result: EpCAMlo signatures from HCT116 and SW480 are highly correlated with each other, with CMS4 signature genes, and with the CCS3 mesenchymal-like cell line signature.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A using the CMS3232 cohort. The high correlations validate the biological relevance of the EpCAMlo phenotype to mesenchymal colon cancer subtypes.

results.result: High expression of EpCAMlo signatures identifies primary colon cancer patients with high metastatic propensity and significantly shorter overall survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C49 are supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in Figure 4C using the CMS3232 cohort. The prognostic value of the signatures demonstrates clinical relevance of the EpCAMlo phenotype.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing analyzed more than 1000 cells from each EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi subpopulation at approximately 50,000 reads per cell.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is stated in the methods and represents adequate sequencing depth and cell numbers for scRNAseq analysis using 10X Genomics technology.

results.result: Unsupervised tSNE analysis shows distinct clustering of EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi cells in HCT116, while SW480 shows partial overlap and a distinct 'spheres' subpopulation; supervised analysis using EMT signature clearly resolves both subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by tSNE analysis in Figure 5A and supervised analysis in Figure 5B. The identification of the 'spheres' population is validated by cited references and signature analysis.

results.result: HCT116 shows a clear EMT transition with minority 'in-between' cells with high pEMT scores, while SW480 shows higher intercellular variance during the transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C54 and C55 are supported by EMT score analysis of scRNAseq data. The differences between cell lines suggest distinct trajectories through EMT states.

results.result: Gene expression trends over the EMT axis show expected patterns: epithelial markers (EPCAM, CDH1) decrease, mesenchymal markers (ZEB1, VIM) increase, and Wnt target genes (AXIN2, DKK1) and Wnt signaling score increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by gene expression trend analysis in Figure 5D. The patterns validate the EMT axis definition and demonstrate coordinated regulation of epithelial, mesenchymal, and Wnt pathway genes.

results.result: SPARC expression peaks at intermediate EMT states, indicative of a partial EMT state.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by SPARC expression trend analysis in Figure 5D. This finding identifies SPARC as a marker of partial EMT states rather than fully mesenchymal cells.

results.result: RNA velocity analysis reveals that most cells remain in their respective states with both states containing source and sink points, EpCAMlo cells are more likely to transit to EpCAMhi, and only a small population is captured transitioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by RNA velocity analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D and Figure 5E. The analysis is consistent with the Markov model predictions and demonstrates the dynamic nature of the system.

results.result: The plastic population of transitioning cells shows the highest pEMT score and high SPARC expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C64 and C65 are supported by pEMT score projection in Figure 5F and SPARC expression in Figure 5G. This identifies a specific transitioning population with distinct molecular features.

results.result: Unsupervised clustering reveals 8 subclusters (3 EpCAMhi, 5 EpCAMlo) with four distinct gene sets expressed in different combinations, including mes1 (ZEB1, VIM, SNAI2) throughout EpCAMlo clusters and mes2 (SPARC, FN1, TWIST1) in pEMT cluster #7.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by unsupervised clustering in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and k-means clustering in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F. The analysis reveals transcriptional heterogeneity and distinct routes through which pEMT cells arise.

results.result: SPARC overexpression increases EMT-TF expression (ZEB1, SNAI2), alters epithelial/mesenchymal marker expression, and enhances motility and invasive capacity of EpCAMlo cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by qPCR and migration assay data in Figure 5H. This functional validation demonstrates that SPARC can actively promote EMT and invasive properties.

results.result: The CMS4_RF signature shows highest association with stromal cells in scRNAseq data, is enriched in CMS4 tumors, and is associated with poor survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by scRNAseq analysis in Figure 6A, bulk RNAseq in Figure 6B, and survival analysis in Figure 6C. This validates that the original CMS4 signature primarily reflects stromal contamination.

results.result: The tumor cell-specific CMS4_TC signature shows highest association with epithelial tumor cells, is enriched in CMS1 and CMS4 tumors, outperforms CMS4_RF in survival stratification, and can stratify CMS1 and CMS3 patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 are supported by scRNAseq analysis in Figure 6D, bulk RNAseq in Figure 6E, and survival analyses in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The CMS4_TC signature successfully identifies tumor cell-intrinsic mesenchymal features with prognostic value across CMS subtypes.

results.result: Mesenchymal-like tumor cells represent 9.7% of all tumor cells in scRNAseq data, with highest association to CMS4_TC signature in CMS1 and CMS4 patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C82 are supported by annotation of scRNAseq data from Lee et al., 2020 shown in Figure 6G. This identifies the frequency and distribution of mesenchymal-like tumor cells in primary tumors.

results.result: Mesenchymal-like tumor cells show lower EPCAM expression and higher expression of CD44, VIM, COL1A1, MMP7, ECM1, and SPARC compared to bulk tumor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C83 and C84 are supported by differential expression analysis in Figure 6H. The expression pattern validates that mesenchymal-like cells in primary tumors resemble the EpCAMlo cells characterized in cell lines.

results.result: HCT116 and SW480 are representative of the microsatellite instability (MIN) and chromosomal instability (CIN/MSS) colon cancer subtypes, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C86 are supported by cited reference (Lengauer et al., 1997) and represent established knowledge about these cell lines. This justifies their selection for studying EMT across different colon cancer subtypes.

results.result: Background claims establish the conceptual framework: the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, role of epigenetic changes in plasticity, EMT and stem cell features, the mCSC model, β-catenin paradox, prior observations in breast and oral cancer, CMS4 characteristics, partial EMT, SPARC function, and CTCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C103 represent established knowledge from cited literature that provides context for the study. These are appropriately cited and represent the scientific foundation for the experimental work.
